Dr Bashir Ullah DAG with Md Mostafa Jamal, DAG, Kazi Md Mahmudul Karim, AAG and Md Shafiquzzaman, AAG-------For the State.

full_judgment:
SM Mozibur Rahman J: On an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the Rule was issued calling  upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and order No. 14 dated 13-5-2015 passed by the learned Special Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka in Special Criminal Revision No. 11 of 2014 setting aside the order No. 28 dated 18-9-2013 passed by the learned Court of Metropolitan Magistrate, 21st Court, Dhaka in Motijheel PS Case No. 5(6) 2009 arising out of Petition Case No. 166 of 2009 under sections 420/406 of the Penal Code rejecting the 2nd naraji petition of the complainant should not be quashed and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Short facts necessary for disposal of the Rule, are that that the complainant opposite party No. 2 filed a petition of complaint before the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka alleging inter alma that the accused-petitioner issued a cheque of Taka 3,40,37,791 in favour of the complainant on 28-6-2008. The complainant opposite party No. 2 as per instruction of the petitioner, deposited the cheque in the concerned bank three times for encashment, but it was dishonoured due to insufficiency of fund in the account of the accused-petitioner on 29-6-2008, 20-7-2008 and 27-9-2009. As a result, the complainant could not seek redress of section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act due to the expiry of time specified for filing a complaint case reckoning date from sending a demand notice for payment of cheque money after the first date of dishonour of cheque. 

 3. Subsequently, complainant opposite party No. 2 filed a petition of complaint against the accused-petitioner on 26-5-2009 under sections 420/406 of the Penal Code upon which learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka sent the complaint petition to the Motijheel Police Station directing the Officer-in-Charge of the Motijheel Police Station to treat it as a First Information Report. Thereafter Officer-in-Charge of the Motijheel Police Station after investigation submitted final report and prayed for discharging the accused-persons from the case. Against this final report complainant bank submitted naraji petition and after hearing this naraji petition learned Metropolitan Magistrate allowed the same and further directed the Officer-in-Charge of the Motijheel Police Station for further investigation. Subsequently, the new investigation Officer after concluding investigation again submitted second final report praying for discharging the accused-persons from the case. The complainant bank again preferred naraji petition against this final report and after hearing the said naraji petition the learned Metropolitan Magistrate 21st Court, Dhaka rejected the naraji petition and accepted the final report No. 58 dated 21-6-2013 dis-charging the accused-persons from the case vide Order No. 28 dated 18-9-2013. Against this order passed by the learned Metropolitan Magistrate complainant bank filed the revisional application before the learned Metropolitan Sessions Judge Court, Dhaka who transferred the case record to the court of learned Special Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka for disposal. The learned Special Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka after hearing both the parties set-aside the Order No. 28 dated 18-9-2013 passed by the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, 21st Court, Dhaka and directed the learned Metropolitan Magistrate to proceed with the case in accordance with law. At this stage the petitioner filed the instant quashment petition and obtained Rule. 

 4. Mr Faysal Mustafa, the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner at the time of submission referred to the following cases:— 

 5. Citing the cases as has been stated above, learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner submits that the allegations of bouncing of cheque simpliciter does not ipso facto constitute any offence as defined under section 115 of the Penal Code which is punishable under section 420 of the said Code and, as such, taking cognizance against the petitioner under section 420 of the Penal Code shall suffer from serious illegality. Learned Advocate further submits that with regard to constitute the offence of criminal breach of trust, there must be dishonest misappropriation by any person in whom confidence is placed as to the custody or management of the property in respect of which the breach of trust is charged. In the instant case there is nothing in the FIR to show that the accused-petitioner had dishonest or fraudulent intention at the time of committing the alleged offence and therefore the impugned judgment and order is illegal and is an abuse of the process of the court. Lastly learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that since the contentions made in the FIR do not come within the purview of sections 420/406 of the Penal Code, it is apparently seen to be a dispute of civil nature for which the whole proceeding is liable to be quashed in terms of cited cases as has been mentioned above. 

 6. On the other hand Mr A Al-Masud Begh, the learned Advocate for the complainant opposite party No. 2 submits that the statements made in paragraph Nos. 1-8 of the application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure are matters of fact and record which required to be proved at the time of trial. In course of exercising extra-ordinary jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court Division cannot decide the factual aspect of the case and, as such, the statements are misleading, misconceived, misconception of law which are not tenable in the eye of law. Learned Advocate further submits that a prima facie case of criminal offence having been made out as per contention made in the petition of complaint which has been subsequently converted as an FIR the High Court Division in course of exercising its extra ordinary jurisdiction has little scope to scrutinize the truth of any document or other evidence which may be used as a defence plea in a criminal proceeding. Hence at this stage when cognizance of offence has not yet been taken against the accused-petitioner, quashment of the proceedings is not permissible. Lastly with regard to Artha Rin Adalat Ain, learned Advocate submits that it is an established principles of law that there is no bar in proceeding with the case filed under sections 420/406 of the Penal Code simultaneously with the proceedings under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. An offence committed under sections 420/406 of the Penal Code is for imposing punishment to the offender while Artha Rin Adalat relates to realization of defaulted loan amount by way of following Civil Procedure Code, 1908. So, the learned Special Judge committed no illegality in passing the respective order and, as such, the impugned order is not liable to be quashed. 

 7. In view of the above submissions of the learned Advocates for both the sides, we have perused the quashment petition and all other relevant papers appended thereto. We have also perused the petition filed under sections 420/406 of the Penal Code before the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate of the petitioner that the cheque was issued as part payment of the loan liability as alleged by the complainant bank and, as such, he prayed for discharging the accused-persons from the case on the ground that in case of civil liability, criminal proceeding should not be allowed to continue. Accordingly, the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka allowed the petition and discharged the accused person from the case against which informant filed a revisional application before the learned Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Dhaka who transferred the case record to the Special Judge 6th Court, Dhaka for trial and disposal. Thereafter the learned Special Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka after hearing the parties set-aside the order passed by the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate by his judgment and order passed in Criminal Revision case No. 11 of 2014. At this stage, the accused-petitioner filed the instant quashment petition and obtained the Rule. 

 8. In this quashment petition we have carefully examined the ground set forth by the accused-petitioner along with the judgment and order passed by the learned Special Sessions Judge in Criminal Revision No. 11 of 2014. But we do not find any such ground that has been specifically mentioned in this quashment petition relying upon which we can interfere with the order passed by the learned Special Sessions Judge, Dhaka who after setting aside the order of the Metropolitan Magistrate, asked him only to proceed with the case as per law. Admittedly, the case is under investigation stage and before conclusion of further investigation this quashment petition has been filed. So, we do not find any reasonable cause to interfere with this unimpeachable order of the learned Special Sessions Judge, as he passed in Criminal Revision No. 11 of 2004. On the other hand in the case of Aminul Islam vs Mujibur Rahman, reported in 45 DLR (AD) 9, it was decided by their lordship that the jurisdiction under section 561A cannot be invoked for the purpose of examining the correctness, legality or propriety of any findings, sentence or order recorded or passed by any inferior criminal court which is done in exercise of revisional jurisdiction under sections 435/439/439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. A revision petition cannot be brought before the High Court Division in the camouflage of a petition under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Good or bad, the finding as recorded by the learned Magistrate or learned Special Sessions Judge which was in accordance with law ought not to have been interfered with under section 561A, for, it has already been indicated that the scope of interference under the said section is very limited. 

 9. In view of the discussion made above and considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we do not find any merit in this Rule. In the result, the Rule is discharged.
